Some favorites include Joel McHale, Charlie Cox, Jennifer Garner, Tina Fey, Kate Winslet, Bob Odenkirk, Andy Richter, Jordan Schlansky, Jamie Dornan, Yeardley Smith, Rafe Spall, Esther Smith, and a reasonable toss-up between Cookie Monster and Kermit the Frog. Running a hotel is already hard enough without the threat of shadowy ghosts swallowing up your guests. Thankfully, only one single mom shares that burden with her dead brother, two kids, and a demon stuck in a little Victorian boy’s body in Netflix’s Haunted Hotel. Yet somehow, amid the chaos they’re so used to, it’s a witch’s cursed soup that catches the four off guard after a nut allergy sends one of the children to the hospital. Hilariously, the witch is also admitted for a nasty cough that needs some medicine attention, proving even evil has to deal with its health.

That ridiculous detour captures the best of Matt Roller’s adult animated comedy (executive produced by Dan Harmon), which is also one of this season’s best returns to streaming. With laugh-out-loud writing and sharper emotional beats, Season 2 turns everyday headaches into some strange, yet endearing jokes. Even with just eight episodes this season as opposed to last year’s 10, Haunted Hotel still gives its characters room to grow, which is the fun (and more emotional) part. With plenty of shenanigans and heart, the result is a humorous, bloody return to the Undervale that earns its surprisingly tender moments.

After getting a handle on the hotel’s initial vibes in Season 1, Katherine (Eliza Coupe) has finally settled into running the Undervale, though finding reliable help remains a challenge. With a lot on his mind this time around, her brother Nathan (Will Forte) continues to pitch in alongside a growing collection of ghosts who need their issues answered. But along the way, her children have their own problems: Ben (Skyler Gisondo) is still dating his ghost girlfriend, Annabelle (Riki Lindhome), but discovers a relationship across different eras is not easy, whereas his younger sister Esther (Natalie Palamides) gets deeper into dark magic. There also comes a point when her confidence begins to outpace her carefulness, which becomes especially dangerous this season.

Adding to the recklessness is Abaddon (Jimmi Simpson), who has become a regular part of the household and basically Katherine’s other child despite his demonic habits. The fights he has with Esther and a growing interest in Ben give him plenty to do beyond causing trouble. New arrivals, including an eager hotel helper and a Constantine-type visitor claiming he can save the world, keep everyone at the Undervale busy and on their toes, especially Nathan, who is forced to feel his feelings more than once.
‘Haunted Hotel’ Season 2 Makes Its Characters Worth Caring About

With those relationships now fully established in Season 2, the writing builds jokes around what each character wants. In one episode, Abaddon’s quest for mac and cheese turns a missing dinner into a crisis worthy of his dramatic gifts. Meanwhile, Katherine’s need for help leads to a many-armed concierge that makes her job easier until its methods become a problem and, unfortunately, hurt Ben. The situations are absurd, but the frustrations are easy to recognize. The show also lets its best jokes end without ever explaining them, and it’s that trust in the audience that keeps the pace brisk, even when an episode has several stories running.

Simpson’s Abaddon remains a standout. His deadpan delivery demands sound perfectly reasonable as the demon child, which is half the fun and a testament to very specific writing. But his character’s softer side is just as effective, especially when he shares a tender episode with Katherine. But Forte gets the strongest material as Nathan. His reluctance to open up to a ghost support group plants the first hints of sadness that the season takes time to explore, especially after his suicide. In the midseason episode, a rare chance to leave the grounds lets him enjoy activities like standing in a grocery line, which turns into a Before Sunrise date where he briefly imagines life with a lighthouse ghost named Bridget (Zooey Deschanel). Through Forte, the writing brilliantly shifts between Nathan’s excitement and fear, feeling painfully natural without ever treating him as someone to pity.

Roller and his team of writers, including Avital Ash and Alix Bloom, build on all of that for the finale with flashbacks of Nathan creating the Undervale. It’s a tender montage that begins with the odd pleasures of renovating alongside ghosts, but then grows harder to watch as time passes and visitors fail to arrive, including his sister and her kids. The hotel becomes a record of his effort and isolation, most sadly when we see the flashes of an ambulance outside the grounds. But when he and Katherine finally express how happy they are to have each other despite him now being a ghost, the simple exchange needs no grand speech. The writers have already shown what her presence means to him through every interaction they have this season, and it’s a moving payoff that trusts a few simple words to carry the weight of everything.
‘Haunted Hotel’ Season 2 Keeps Its Horrors Visually Inventive

With returning animation from Titmouse, Inc., the series’ visuals give its monsters a real bite. They move quickly and smoothly, making something as simple as a tunnel chase feel more dangerous even with Esther and Abaddon bickering. The purple ooze that spreads throughout the building, while bloody vines turn the woods into another place to avoid, adds to Haunted Hotel’s realistic scares and charm. Not to mention, these threats have enough presence to hold viewers' attention between punchlines.

But it’s not all thrills and chills, as the quiet details are just as effective. Ghosts lurk in corners and shadows, at least in one episode, adding another layer of creepiness a show like this needs. Those figures also reward a closer look without needing a big entrance, reminding us to check out the whole picture, as Titmouse, Inc. does a strong job of telling the entire story in a single frame. Best of all, its visual comedy works really well. Nathan trying to rescue the boys from hungry mermaids, only to sink through the water because ghosts cannot swim, makes terrific and hilarious use of his physical limits. While we see his eagerness help set up the gag, it’s the animation that delivers the failure cleanly.

Through vibrant and visually bold details, Haunted Hotel’s second season makes its busy premise surprisingly easy to manage and stay engaged. A few thinner detours keep it from being great across the board, but its strongest episodes and sharp writing show how much this odd household has to offer. With brilliant jokes, inventive scares, and a few moments that really sting, Haunted Hotel makes a second stay at the Undervale well worth it.
Haunted Hotel is now streaming on Netflix.
Bob Suarez, Meg Waldow, Christopher Nance, Erica Hayes
Matt Roller, Avital Ash, Joshua Corey, Siena East, Dan Guterman
The writing finds fresh laughs in ordinary family problems, letting curses, demons, and hotel disasters complicate situations that already feel familiar.
Nathan's story gives the season its emotional weight, with Will Forte making his excitement, loneliness, and love for Katherine feel equally convincing.
Titmouse's animation makes the hotel feel dangerous, with fast-moving monsters, bloody vines, and ghosts hiding in corners that reward a closer look.
Some side adventures lack the depth of the main family stories.
